messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 46

Carlos remembers the earth moving. That morning in 1960 had started like any other in his small coastal town in Chile—the salt air, the roosters, his mother humming as she folded laundry. When the shaking began, he was eight years old, clutching the leg of a wooden table as the floor buckled beneath him. For three minutes, the world tore itself apart. He watched the house across the street fold into itself like paper. He heard his mother scream his name, then the sound of plaster and wood drowning her out. When it stopped, she was gone. The tsunami came later, sweeping away what little remained.

Carlos never spoke about that day. He didn’t cry at the funeral, and he didn’t cry years later when his father moved them to Santiago. He learned to keep his head down, to look for cracks before they spread. That skill carried him into a career as a QA engineer—a profession built on vigilance, on catching the fault before the system fails. At 75, he still works part-time for a software firm in Miami, checking code for bugs that might cost the company millions. He is good at it. Too good, his wife Marta sometimes says, because he checks the same module four times before signing off.

The symptoms didn’t surface until after he retired the first time, at 70. Without the structure of work, the quiet crept in, and with it, the feeling that the ground might shift at any moment. He started sleeping poorly—waking at 3:17 a.m. every night, convinced he felt a tremor. The bedroom door must be open, the hallway clear, the exit route unobstructed. He insists on sleeping with his shoes next to the bed. Marta thinks it’s a habit from his army days; he never corrects her.

He avoids the news, especially weather reports. When a hurricane warning is issued, he becomes short-tempered and withdrawn. He packs a go-bag with water, flashlights, and a copy of his mother’s photograph, the only one he saved. He places it in the same spot every time—the second shelf of the hall closet, behind the winter coats. He checks it twice a day until the storm passes.

At work, his vigilance has become obsessive. He runs test scripts three times instead of once. He flags minor anomalies that other engineers ignore. His manager smiles and calls him thorough, but Carlos knows why: *because if you miss one crack, the whole thing comes down.* Last week, a loud truck backfired outside the office. He dropped his coffee, his heart hammering, and spent the next hour in the bathroom, steadying himself against the sink.

On weekends, he sits in the back yard with a cup of cold tea, staring at the sky. Marta brings him a blanket. He jumps at her touch. He doesn’t tell her that sometimes, when the wind picks up, he hears wood splintering and a woman screaming his name. He doesn’t tell her that the ground feels solid, but he never trusts it. Not really. Not since he was eight.
